# Where this material lives

Nothing was lost. The preamble drafted on 4 September 2026 is at
`publishing/preamble-draft.md` and is committed. It was never rendered because
it is a planning file rather than a chapter, so the book project does not build
it, which is why it is absent from `_out`. This document gathers it together
with the other places the book's wider perspective is written down, so the whole
of the argument can be read in one sitting.

Four files carry it, and each has a different job.

`publishing/preamble-draft.md` holds the preamble itself and the author
biography. `publishing/book-spine.md` holds the single thread that runs through
every chapter, with its 5 September amendment. `index.qmd` is the preface as it
currently stands in the book. `publishing/book-proposal.md` holds the same
argument in the register a publisher reads.

\newpage

# The preamble

This book teaches the measurement of forest carbon from satellite and airborne
observation, and it teaches it from the beginning. That second half of the
sentence is a deliberate choice and it is worth explaining before you read
further, because it is what separates this book from most of what sits beside it
on the shelf.

The remote sensing literature is superb and it starts in the middle. Open almost
any recent volume on forest observation and the first chapter maps canopy height
from radar, or fuses Sentinel-1 with Sentinel-2 to model aboveground biomass, or
corrects the geolocation of spaceborne laser footprints. Every one of those
chapters is excellent and every one assumes you already know what a coordinate
reference system does to an area calculation, why a time series is a
three-dimensional object rather than a stack of pictures, and where the
uncertainty in a reported tonne actually comes from. The methods literature will
teach you to project a raster and never mention what a verifier does with the
result. The standards documents start on the far side of the same gap and will
tell you that an uncertainty deduction is required without ever showing you how
to compute one. In practice the two are reconciled in undocumented spreadsheets,
and that is where forest monitoring systems fail. They fail from inaccessible
workflows and thin documentation far more often than they fail from flawed
science.

So this book walks a trajectory rather than presenting a collection. The early
chapters put a shapefile and a raster in your hands, establish what a projection
does to a hectare, and settle what support means before any number is reported.
Those chapters are not remedial. The errors that end up costing a project its
credits are almost always made in the first hour of the work, in a
transformation nobody wrote down or a mask applied in the wrong order, and by the
time they surface in an audit they are buried under six months of analysis that
looks impeccable. Building the foundation slowly is the cheapest uncertainty
reduction available. Each chapter then adds one layer and closes on a defensible
number, so that by the final part a reader who began by reading a shapefile is
propagating allometric error through a Monte Carlo simulation and converting the
result into the credits a project forgoes for being imprecise.

Everything here runs. The book is written in Quarto, every figure and every
number in the text is generated by code that ships with it, and the whole thing
builds offline on a laptop with no account, no cloud credit and no network. That
is not a convenience. A verifier has to be able to re-run your work three years
later on a different machine, and an analysis that cannot be re-run has not been
documented, only described. Where a registry document is cited the citation is to
the section and the equation, so a reader can check it against the original
rather than take my word for it.

What I hope carries through all of it is the reason any of us do this work.
There is a particular pleasure in looking at a planet you have only ever stood on
and slowly acquiring the tools to map it, to measure it, and to say something
about it that holds up, and I have tried to write a book that keeps hold of that
rather than assuming the reader arrived already fluent.

# The spine

Recorded 4 September 2026 and amended 5 September 2026. This is the thread that
opens in chapter 1, is picked up in every chapter, and closes in the final part.
It exists so that no chapter can be written without knowing what it owes the arc.

## The thread

**The geometry you compute on, and the support your answer has.**

Both halves are needed and they are not the same question. Geometry is where the
arithmetic happens, on a plane, on a sphere, on an ellipsoid, in a projected grid
that distorts area with latitude. Support is what the answer refers to, the area
or the interval or the volume over which a value was measured and to which it
applies. Every number in forest carbon accounting has both, almost no report
states either, and the errors that survive to an audit are nearly always one of
them.

It is the only question that is genuinely present in every chapter, from reading
a shapefile to reporting a deduction, and it is the question the field's own
literature treats as settled and does not.

## Where it now closes

Amended 5 September 2026. The closing message of the book is disturbance
ecology, and the spatio-temporal data cube is the instrument that makes it
arguable rather than the destination. By the final part the reader has a cube fit
for spatial modelling, and the question the book then asks of it is whether a
forest carbon landscape has states, whether it can pass between them, and whether
a monitoring system built from these observations could tell. That takes the
argument into bifurcation and tipping behaviour, regime shift in ecosystem change
and forest carbon flux, and Markov chain Monte Carlo as the machinery for
inference about a dynamical system observed with error.

That does not displace the design-based against model-based distinction after
Pebesma. It subsumes it, because asking whether a system has changed regime is a
question about what the data can support, and the honest answer needs the
inferential frame the earlier chapters built. The sentence a reader should be
able to say at the end is that they know the geometry, the support, the
inferential frame, and what all three together permit them to claim about whether
the forest is the same forest.

## The closing move

The last chapter returns explicitly to the first. The reader is shown the same
polygon from chapter 1 and asked what its area is now, and the honest answer is
that it depends on the geometry, the engine, the support and the inferential
frame, all four of which they can now state. That is the arc, and it is the
difference between a book that teaches operations and one that teaches judgement.

# The house rule for chapters

Every chapter enters through something concrete and physical, reaches a
methodological question by the middle, closes on a number a verifier would
accept, and states somewhere what geometry the arithmetic happened on and what
support the answer has.

Each one carries a single methodological question, an entry that earns its place,
and an edge that does not flinch. The board at
<https://claude.ai/code/artifact/4499bb90-ae13-4fdd-8051-ee6e63d01c74> holds all
seventeen with their questions, their entries, their edges and their sources.

# The book in one paragraph

From `publishing/book-proposal.md`, kept here because it is the same argument in
the register a publisher reads.

Carbon projects are audited on numbers that come out of a geographic information
system, and almost nobody who audits them was trained to build one. This book
teaches the spatial analysis that forest carbon verification actually rests on,
from reading a shapefile to reporting an uncertainty deduction, and it does so
with the primary registry documents open beside the code.

# Open decisions

Four, all recorded on the chapter board and none of them settled.

1. Does one of the last chapters carry the dynamical-systems close explicitly?
   The seventeen-chapter outline as briefed spreads it across chapters 12, 13 and
   the closing part, so no chapter owns it and none is accountable for it.
2. Does the subtitle going to Elsevier name disturbance ecology? It currently
   promises lidar, radar and optical data in mensuration, monitoring and
   inventory, and none of those three is the closing argument.
3. Is the page budget 400 pages or 560? *Satellite Remote Sensing for Forest and
   Environmental Monitoring* runs 20 chapters over 663 pages, so 33 a chapter puts
   seventeen at about 560 before front matter.
4. Does the baseline chapter lose the word *counterfactual*? It appears nine times
   in that chapter's prose and the standing style rule excludes terms imported
   from programme evaluation where the field's own wording exists.
